# Tehisabiline: factual overview

Last materially reviewed: 2026-11-04
Canonical source: https://tehisabiline.ee/
Short index: https://tehisabiline.ee/llms.txt

This file summarizes public website information. The site language is Estonian; this overview is in English. When a statement here and a page disagree, the page is authoritative.

## Entity

- Legal name: Tehisabiline OÜ
- Registered office: Viimsi Parish, Harju County, Estonia (public register: https://ariregister.rik.ee/eng/company/17607255). Registry code 17607255. Service area: Estonia.
- Founder: Arle Aron Reidma (LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/arlearonreidma/). Company profile: https://www.f6s.com/company/tehisabiline
- Email: tehisabiline@gmail.com
- Website: https://tehisabiline.ee/
- Code profile: https://github.com/AARenor/tehisabiline
- Public company facts: https://tehisabiline.ee/ai_info/ (Estonian; source-linked identity, described service scope, API development status, limits and correction route).
- HTML entity map: https://tehisabiline.ee/entitymap/ (Estonian; organization, founder, service nodes, topics and page clusters rendered from entitymap.json).

## Current status

- Public uncensored-model text demo: available as a standalone demo at https://tehisabiline.ee/mudelid/#demo. Its dedicated endpoint is https://ai.tehisabiline.ee/api/demo/chat; it proxies to a same-host local model service.
- The demo has a fixed server-side system prompt and accepts only the current user prompt: no conversation history, RAG, CRM or app-level conversation database. Prompt maximum: 2,000 Unicode characters. Model-generated reasoning, when returned, is streamed separately from the final answer; total output is capped at 4,096 generated tokens, including up to 1,024 reasoning tokens. One generation runs at a time. Rate limits: 5 requests/minute and 20/hour per IP, 100/hour globally.
- The demo route does not log prompt or generated-output content. This does not establish what Cloudflare, the tunnel, model service or runtime infrastructure logs or retains; those practices have not been verified. Users must not submit personal or confidential data. No server-country or third-party non-processing claim is made.
- Commercial cybersecurity API: still planned/in development, not public, with no production endpoint or published price. It is separate from the uncensored-model demo. Model hosting in Estonia is forthcoming for the planned API; hardware has been ordered, but processing there is not live.
- Pentesting and audits: offered for systems the client owns or controls, under written authorization and an agreed scope. Cloud configuration can be included in an agreed scope; no separate network, mobile or cloud speciality, complete OWASP coverage, certificate, fixed price or security guarantee is implied.
- The planned commercial API intends human review for consequential outputs. Demo responses are automatically generated and are not human-reviewed.
- Tehisabiline does not claim 100 percent security, error-free AI, guaranteed savings or guaranteed outcomes.

## Services

### Pentest ja turvatestimine Eestis

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/pentestimine/

Additional Estonian terms: turvatestimine and läbistustestimine. The service page explains who benefits, the decisions testing supports and Tehisabiline's working principles. Every process phase names its output: agreed targets, written authorization, validated findings and report. Quote requests specify the system, test objective, access/staging options, preferred window, retest needs and authorization contact.

Estonian terms: turvatestimine, pentestimine, pentest and läbitungimistest. Tehisabiline offers scoped active security testing of agreed web applications and APIs. It assesses whether weaknesses can be exploited within the authorization, rather than simply repeating scanner warnings. The engagement specifies targets, environment, accounts, allowed actions, test window, stop conditions and contacts before testing. Important findings are reviewed by a human. Outputs include evidence, impact, recommended fixes and the retest agreed in the offer. Pricing depends on targets, roles, flows, access, test depth and follow-up; initial mapping is free. Black-box, grey-box and white-box describe the information supplied to the tester and are scoping choices, not guaranteed packages. OWASP WSTG and NIST SP 800-115 are referenced as public planning guidance, not certifications.

### Pentesti raporti näidis

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/pentestimine/naidisraport/

A clearly synthetic sample report showing what a buyer should expect: tested scope and limitations, PTES/OWASP-based methodology, three findings with masked evidence and impact, a remediation plan ordered by immediate/7-day/planned, and retest conditions. All names, domains and findings are fictitious; it is not a client report and does not claim a real engagement.

### TLPT / TIBER-EE

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/tlpt/

Explains DORA Article 26 threat-led penetration testing and Estonia's TIBER-EE implementation (Finantsinspektsioon guidance in force 15.09.2026): designated entities, TCT-EE coordination, threat intelligence, red/blue team exercise, attestation and confidentiality. It distinguishes TLPT from a normal pentest and states that Tehisabiline does not present itself as a TIBER-EE tester.

### DORA guide

Guide to DORA in Estonia: scope follows the Article 2 list rather than "the financial sector"; the five pillars (ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, third-party risk and information sharing); Finantsinspektsioon supervision; the incident-reporting channel: the Eesti Pank and Finantsinspektsioon data-collection portal from 1 November 2026, e-mail before that; the Article 28(3) register of information, submitted as an annual summary with the full register on request and a year-end collection on 31.12.2026; a downloadable CSV register template; TLPT under Articles 26–27 via TIBER-EE with attestation by Finantsinspektsioon or the ECB; differences from NIS2 and E-ITS; and a four-step preparation order. It states that DORA has no certificate and is not limited to pentesting, that DORA is a regulation rather than a directive and therefore needed no transposition, and that the technical detail sits in delegated and implementing regulations 2024/1774 (ICT risk management), 2024/1773 (contracts supporting critical or important functions), 2025/1190 (TLPT) and 2024/2956 (register templates).

### Articles

Hub with practical guides. The backup restore-test article covers RPO/RTO, test scope and levels, a 90-minute test plan, metrics and NIS2 evidence. The NIS2 supply-chain article covers supplier tiering, due diligence, contract clauses, ongoing review and evidence. The MFA rollout article compares FIDO2/passkeys, TOTP, push and SMS, prioritises critical accounts, handles legacy systems and break-glass access, defines coverage metrics and gives a 30/60/90-day plan.

The NIS2 board-duties article covers the management body’s approval and oversight role, the evidence it should see, a 45–60 minute agenda, questions to ask and a 90-day plan. The cyber risk-register article covers register columns, a 5×5 assessment, treatment and residual risk, evidence, a downloadable CSV template and a 30/60/90-day plan.

### E-ITS (Estonian information security standard)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/e-its/

Explains the Estonian information security standard administered by RIA: it is set by regulation no. 30 (25.08.2026, in force 01.09.2026), mandatory for public-sector tasks, applied to KüTS service providers as the basic measures, and added when those basic measures are not sufficient; otherwise its use is voluntary. Covers E-ITS audit versus ISO 27001 certification; filing deadlines are distinct: the auditee submits the audit conclusion to the supervisory authority within 14 days of receiving both the conclusion and final report (audit rule 6.17), while Government Regulation no. 121 § 4(2) separately requires the service provider to forward the conclusion to RIA within 30 days of receiving it. Observe both requirements and meet the earlier applicable deadline. For a high-level risk, the final report is also submitted and the risk must be remedied within six months. Covers a six-step evidence preparation path. It explicitly states that an E-ITS audit is not a pentest, not an ISO certificate, and not a service Tehisabiline performs as a formal E-ITS audit.

### AI application security testing

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/ai-turvatestimine/

Scoped security testing of LLM, RAG and agent applications: direct and indirect prompt injection, retrieval/tenant leakage, tool permissions and excessive agency, output handling, API/key abuse and third-party model supply chain. The page states limits: probabilistic behaviour, sample-based coverage, no AI Act conformity certificate and no testing of a model provider without permission. AI Act Article 15 and NIS2 are framed as evidence and governance context, not as a guarantee.

### Turvaaudit / küberaudit / cybersecurity audit

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/kuberaudit/

Tehisabiline offers cybersecurity audits and scoped penetration testing for Estonian businesses. The same service is described in Estonian as turvaaudit, küberaudit, IT turvaaudit, küberturbe audit or infoturbe audit; the page distinguishes broad security-posture review from penetration testing and certification. Audits cover agreed website, API and AI-application checks and give a broader view of security posture; a pentest tests whether a weakness can be exploited within the agreed target. Automated scanning alone is not equivalent to either service. Written authorization, targets, permitted tests and stop conditions are agreed before active testing. A human reviews significant findings; the client receives evidence, a prioritized remediation plan and the re-check agreed in the offer. Price depends on scope, depth, access and re-check needs; initial mapping is free. No fixed public price or guaranteed security outcome is claimed.

### Standalone uncensored-model public text demo

Canonical entry point: https://tehisabiline.ee/mudelid/#demo
Dedicated endpoint: https://ai.tehisabiline.ee/api/demo/chat

This public text demo is a standalone technical demonstration and is not the planned commercial cybersecurity API. The endpoint uses a fixed server-side system prompt and sends only the current prompt to the same-host local model service. Each request has no conversation history, RAG or CRM. The route does not log prompt or generated-output content or use an app-level conversation database. Responses stream; only one generation runs at a time; prompts are limited to 2,000 Unicode characters and total output is capped at 4,096 generated tokens, including up to 1,024 reasoning tokens. When the model returns reasoning, the page displays it separately from the final answer. Limits are 5 requests/minute and 20/hour per IP, and 100/hour globally.

Cloudflare, tunnel, model and runtime infrastructure logging and retention have not been verified. Do not submit personal or confidential information. No claim is made about server country or third-party non-processing. Neutral public naming does not guarantee that the model will not identify itself in an answer.

### Planned OpenAI-compatible cybersecurity API

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/mudelid/

The commercial API is in development and not public. OpenAI chat-completions compatibility is planned; example code is illustrative, not a working public endpoint. Interested developers can email tehisabiline@gmail.com with their tool, use case and anticipated usage to discuss pilot participation. Actual endpoint, model name, key, limits and pricing are agreed for the pilot; none should be inferred from the examples. Model hosting in Estonia is forthcoming for this planned API; hardware has been ordered, but this processing is not live. Intended models support security work such as log, code and configuration analysis; significant outputs require human review.

Keeldudeta is Tehisabiline's intended model positioning: support for legitimate security work within agreed legal and authorization boundaries, not unrestricted or unauthorized activity. This planned API is the second main offering alongside the cybersecurity audit/pentesting service; it is not the standalone uncensored-model demo.

## Other public pages

### Homepage

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/

Overview of cybersecurity audit/pentesting for businesses, the planned developer API and a separate public uncensored-model text demo. The commercial cybersecurity API remains in development, not public; the demo is not that API. Both API testing of a client's existing system and the planned model API are distinct.

### API security testing guide

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/api-turvatestimine/

API turvatestimine, API pentest and API penetration testing concern testing a client's existing API, not Tehisabiline's planned model API. The guide covers object/function authorization, authentication, field visibility, resource controls, business flows and API inventory. A synthetic role/tenant matrix and authorized BOLA/IDOR scenario illustrate expected access boundaries and redacted evidence. Preparation includes API documentation, test accounts, synthetic data, ownership/permission, exclusions and limits. Source: OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/.

### Web application security testing guide

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/veebirakenduse-turvatestimine/

Veebirakenduse turvatestimine, veebilehe pentest and web application penetration testing concern agreed web user flows and server-side access boundaries. The guide covers login, roles, sessions, input handling, configuration and e-commerce workflows, with test accounts, synthetic orders and payment sandbox preparation. It distinguishes scanners, authenticated pentests and broader audits and explains report/retest limits. The illustrated order-access scenario is synthetic, not a customer finding. Source: OWASP WSTG v4.2, https://wstg.owasp.org/v4.2/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/.

### Cyber-AI use cases

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/kasutusjuhud/

Twelve planned pilot use cases (hypotheses) for cyber-AI in security work, each with the human checkpoint and the measure to watch; they are proposals, not measured results. References include MITRE ATT&CK (https://attack.mitre.org/), OWASP LLM Top 10 (https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/) and NCSC guidance (https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blogs/managing-the-cyber-risk-of-agentic-ai).

### API pentest checklist

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/api-turvatestimine/kontrollnimekiri/

The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) evidence table: which check applies, what evidence the report must contain and what a retest verifies. Preparation, test accounts and the access matrix stay on the parent guide.

### NIS2 guide

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/nis2/

Guide to NIS2 in Estonia, which applies through the Cybersecurity Act (KüTS) since 1 January 2026 (current consolidated text RT I, 06.10.2026, 2; https://www.riigiteataja.ee/akt/106102026002). It explains who is in scope under KüTS §3: a list of categories plus a size test (important entities generally have at least 50 employees AND turnover or balance sheet above EUR 10 million; essential entities in the listed categories have at least 250 employees AND balance sheet above EUR 43 million or turnover above EUR 50 million; some categories apply regardless of size). It includes a four-question self-check that runs locally in the browser, the registration route with RIA through eesti.ee, the ten minimum measures (Directive (EU) 2022/2555, Article 21(2)(a)-(j)), management duties (Article 20; KüTS §6¹), incident reporting (early warning within 24 hours and notification within 72 hours of becoming aware; final report within one month of filing the 72-hour notification; KüTS §8), fine ceilings (up to EUR 10 million or 2%, or EUR 7 million or 1.4%, of the previous financial year's worldwide turnover, whichever is higher; KüTS §18² and §18³), the EIS grant (status checked 27.10.2026) and a comparison with E-ITS and ISO 27001. Ordinary micro and small businesses are generally outside the regime unless a size-independent category applies. Check the page and Riigi Teataja for the current text.

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/nis2/kontrollnimekiri/

Ten-measure NIS2 checklist with the evidence an auditor asks for, a quick win and a typical gap per measure; progress is stored only in the reader's browser.

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/nis2/intsidendist-teatamine/

Significant-incident criteria, the three NIS2 reports (early warning within 24 hours and notification within 72 hours of becoming aware, final report within one month of filing the 72-hour notification), what to include, the Estonian reporting channel, near-miss reporting (voluntary), the separate GDPR breach notification and a browser-only deadline calculator.

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/nis2/registreerimine/

Practical registration guide: who must notify RIA, what to prepare before starting, the eesti.ee form, the three-month deadline for a new entity, the two-week change-notification rule, saving proof and common mistakes. It states that registration is not a certificate of compliance.

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/nis2/audit/
Downloadable Excel evidence register (one row per NIS2 art 21(2) measure, real date fields, result/status drop-downs, per-row overdue highlighting and a summary sheet): https://tehisabiline.ee/assets/downloads/nis2-auditi-toendite-mall.xlsx

NIS2 audit guide: scope across management, risk, the ten measures, supply chain and incidents; an evidence table; interviews, sampling and testing; report contents including findings, evidence, impact, priorities and management response; and the difference from a penetration test. NIS2 does not prescribe one mandatory certificate or audit form.

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/nis2/trahvid/

NIS2 fines and supervision: ceilings of EUR 10 million or 2% for essential entities and EUR 7 million or 1.4% for important entities, calculated on the previous financial year's worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. The page explains that a ceiling is not an expected fine, lists the factors a supervisor weighs, covers management responsibility and links to registration and evidence guidance, and includes a browser-only calculator for the mathematical fine ceiling.

Privacy information covers email inquiries, website technical processing and the standalone uncensored-model demo. The demo accepts one prompt only, has no conversation history/RAG/CRM or app-level conversation database, and its route does not log prompt/generated-output content. Generated reasoning, when returned, is displayed separately from the final answer. Cloudflare, tunnel, model and runtime infrastructure logging and retention have not been verified. Users are told not to submit personal or confidential data. The planned commercial cybersecurity API is separate.

### Regulation map

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/regulatsioonid/

Comparison hub for NIS2/KüTS, DORA, E-ITS, ISO/IEC 27001, AI Act and the Cyber Resilience Act. It covers who each framework applies to, the main obligations, current Estonian deadlines and authorities, how the frameworks overlap, the evidence an audit asks for and a practical starting order. A downloadable CSV compares scope, obligations, deadlines, authorities and official sources.

### Estonia cybersecurity regulations (English)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/regulations/

English overview of NIS2/KüTS, DORA, E-ITS, ISO/IEC 27001, the AI Act and the Cyber Resilience Act in Estonia. It maps service-provider, financial-sector, product and AI roles, explains the 2026–2028 deadlines and lists the evidence regulators and auditors ask for. Estonian is the primary language of the site; English versions exist for selected guides and are linked from the page.

### SBOM

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/sbom/

Guide to software bills of materials in Estonian: CRA and NIS2 supply-chain context, the minimum component fields, SPDX/CycloneDX/SWID trade-offs, build-time generation, versioning, VEX and vulnerability follow-up, common mistakes, and a downloadable CSV template. It explains that an SBOM is an inventory, not proof of security.

### Cyber Resilience Act

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/cra/

Guide to Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 in Estonian: products with digital elements, manufacturer and importer duties, support period of at least five years, SBOM and vulnerability handling, the 11 September 2026 reporting deadlines, conformity assessment and CE marking, and the 11 December 2027 transition. Includes a browser-only product-scope self-check. It explains how CRA differs from NIS2 and ISO 27001 and why a pentest alone does not prove conformity.

### AI Act

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/ai-act/

Guide to the EU AI Act in Estonian: provider and deployer roles, prohibited/high-risk/limited/minimal risk, the amended timeline (including the 2026 omnibus delay of high-risk deadlines), TTJA's future market-surveillance role, Article 15 accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity expectations, a browser-only risk-class self-check and the limits of scoped AI security testing. It is explanatory, not legal advice.

### Kõrge riskiga AI-süsteemid

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/ai-act/korge-riskiga-susteemid/

Estonian guide to the high-risk class of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. It walks Article 6 classification step by step — Annex I product rules versus Annex III use lists — and then takes Annex III area by area, use by use (eight areas, 25 listed uses), with the exclusions the annex itself states. It sets out the Article 6(3) exception with its four cumulative conditions and the rule that an Annex III system performing profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, and it explains the registration that follows from a 6(3) self-assessment. Articles 9–15 are mapped to the technical evidence to produce and keep (risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, instructions for use, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity), followed by the provider and deployer duties (Articles 16, 17, 23–27 including the FRIA), the fine tiers of Article 99 up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7%, and the timeline already used on the hub: Annex III obligations from 2 December 2027 and Annex I product rules from 2 August 2028. The page ships a downloadable worksheet (Excel) with the Annex III classification rows, the Article 9–15 evidence map and a role test. It is explanatory, not legal advice.

### DORA register of information

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/dora/teaberegister/

Practical guide to the DORA Article 28(3) register: the contractual and dependency fields, critical/important function mapping, data locations, subcontractors, exit plans and evidence. It explains that the downloadable CSV is an internal working template, not the official ITS (EU) 2024/2956 submission format, and describes submission through the Finantsinspektsioon portal (annual summary, full register on request) and the checks to run before submitting. A browser-only checker validates required fields, date formats and duplicate IDs without uploading the file.

### ISO/IEC 27001

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/iso-27001/

Guide to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 in the Estonian context: what an ISMS is, the Annex A control set with Amendment 1:2024, Stage 1/Stage 2 certification, surveillance and recertification set by the certification body's accredited scheme, the evidence an auditor asks for, accreditation by EAK, and the difference from E-ITS and NIS2. It notes that the 2013 to 2022 transition completed on 31 October 2025 and that Tehisabiline is not an accredited certification body.

### ISO 27001 auditeerimine

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/iso-27001/auditeerimine/

Estonian guide to auditing an ISO/IEC 27001:2022 ISMS. It separates the three audits: the clause 9.2 internal audit, the accredited certification audit and a second-party audit. For clause 9.2 it lays out the 9.2.1–9.2.2 requirements with the artefact to sample for each, gives a seven-step internal audit method, a clause 4–10 checklist with the evidence to request, the audit report structure with four finding classes, and the ISO/IEC 17021-1 certification cycle: a two-stage initial audit, surveillance at least once a calendar year and no later than 12 months after the certification decision, recertification in the third year, and correction of a major nonconformity within six months after the last day of Stage 2. Audit duration is explained only through the ISO/IEC 17021-1 §9.1.4 factors; no prices or day counts are given. It notes that ISO/IEC 27001 does not require ISO 19011 (its only normative reference is ISO/IEC 27000) and does not require a certified internal auditor, that Annex A is normative but not a list of requirements (point 6.1.3 and the Statement of Applicability), and that an internal audit is neither a certification audit nor a penetration test. The page ships an internal audit workbook (Excel) with the audit programme, every clause 4–10 subclause with its evidence column, a finding register and corrective actions. It states that Tehisabiline is not an accredited certification body.

## Facts to quote

These are international research findings, not measurements of Tehisabiline customers or a risk estimate for an Estonian business. Quote with the original source:

- Human element was present in 62% of breaches. Source: Verizon DBIR 2026 executive summary, page 11, https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/executivebriefs/2026-dbir-executive-summary.pdf (cited on https://tehisabiline.ee/kuberaudit/).
- Vulnerability exploitation accounted for 31% of known initial access vectors in non-Error, non-Misuse breaches. Source: Verizon DBIR 2026 executive summary, page 9, https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/executivebriefs/2026-dbir-executive-summary.pdf (cited on https://tehisabiline.ee/kuberaudit/).
- The global average cost of a data breach is 4.99 million USD, 12% more than the year before. Source: IBM Cost of a Data Breach 2026, https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach (cited on https://tehisabiline.ee/kuberaudit/).

## NIS2 in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/nis2/
NIS2 is Directive (EU) 2022/2555, a unified framework for cybersecurity in 18 critical sectors that replaced Directive 2016/1148 (NIS1); it is a directive, not a regulation, so its duties reach organisations through national law. Estonia transposed NIS2 through the Cybersecurity Act (KüTS), in force since 1 January 2026. Entities already in scope on that date had three months to notify RIA (that window closed in spring 2026); a new service provider has three months from becoming one. The ten minimum measures cover risk analysis, incident handling, continuity, supply chain, secure development, effectiveness testing, hygiene and training, cryptography, human resources and access control, and multi-factor authentication. Incident reports: early warning within 24 hours and notification within 72 hours of becoming aware, final report within one month of filing the 72-hour notification.

## NIS2 compliance checklist (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/nis2/checklist/
The English checklist turns Article 21(2)(a)-(j) into ten rows with what done looks like, the evidence a reviewer requests, the sample that proves the measure operates and the owner, plus a separate row for the Article 20 board duties. Any row where only the policy can be produced, and not the proof, is a gap. A printable CSV with the same eleven rows and blank result, finding, action, due date, status and evidence-location columns is free and ungated: https://tehisabiline.ee/assets/downloads/nis2-compliance-checklist.csv

## CRA in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/cra/
The Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) applies directly in Estonia. Reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026; the main product obligations apply from 11 December 2027. Manufacturers must document components and vulnerabilities (an SBOM), handle vulnerabilities, state a support period of at least five years unless the expected lifetime is shorter, complete conformity assessment and keep technical documentation. CRA reporting uses an early warning within 24 hours, a notification within 72 hours and a final report after a corrective measure or one month after notification; both the Estonian and English CRA pages include browser-only deadline calculators.

## CRA vulnerability reporting (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/cra/vulnerability-reporting/
A manufacturer must report any actively exploited vulnerability in its product with digital elements that it becomes aware of: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware and a notification within 72 hours, both to the CSIRT designated as coordinator and to ENISA through the single reporting platform ENISA operates under Article 16, then a final report no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available (Article 14(2)). A severe incident keeps the 24-hour and 72-hour steps but the final report is due within one month after the incident notification (Article 14(4)). Reporting under Article 14 applies from 11 September 2026; the rest of the regulation, Annex I requirements included, from 11 December 2027 (Article 71). The page separates that reporting duty from the eight Annex I, Part II handling requirements — SBOM, remediation without delay, tests and reviews, publication about fixed vulnerabilities, a coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy, a contact address, secure update distribution and free security updates — with the evidence to keep for each row. It states that Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 never names security.txt and never uses CVE or CVSS: the file format comes from RFC 9116, whose Contact field is mandatory and whose single Expires field must be an RFC 3339 timestamp, and the page ships a browser-only builder that validates those fields and makes no network request. A DOCX template adds a coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy outline and the Annex I, Part II evidence table. Policy targets are the reader's own service levels, not statutory deadlines.

## DORA in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/dora/
DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) applies from 17 January 2025. It is a regulation, not a directive, so it applied directly without transposition, and the technical detail sits in delegated and implementing regulations 2024/1774, 2024/1773, 2025/1190 and 2024/2956. Financial entities must maintain an ICT risk framework, a register of information covering contractual arrangements with ICT third-party providers, contractual safeguards, incident reporting and resilience testing. Certain significant entities must carry out threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) at least every three years.

## AI Act in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/ai-act/
The AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in stages. Prohibitions and AI literacy apply from 2 February 2025; general-purpose AI obligations from 2 August 2025; the general date of application, including the Article 50 transparency rules, is 2 August 2026. As amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, new prohibitions and the Article 50(2) transition for systems already on the market apply from 2 December 2026, Annex III high-risk obligations from 2 December 2027 and Annex I product rules from 2 August 2028. Providers and deployers need an AI inventory, role and risk classification, technical documentation, human-oversight evidence, logging and post-market monitoring.

## High-risk AI systems (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/ai-act/high-risk/
Article 6 classification runs in two branches: a system that is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Annex I product-safety law is high-risk, and a system listed in Annex III is high-risk unless the Article 6(3) exception applies. The page takes the eight Annex III areas use by use, states the annex's own exclusions, sets out the four cumulative Article 6(3) conditions and the rule that profiling of natural persons always makes an Annex III system high-risk, and covers the registration that follows a 6(3) self-assessment. Articles 9–15 become a table of requirements with the technical evidence to produce and keep, from risk management and data governance through documentation, logging, instructions for use, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity; provider and deployer duties (Articles 16, 17, 23–27, FRIA included) and the Article 99 fine tiers up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7% follow. An Excel worksheet carries the Annex III rows, the Article 9–15 evidence map and a role test.

## SBOM for CRA (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/sbom/
The CRA requires manufacturers to identify and document product components and vulnerabilities. A useful SBOM is tied to a release, covers transitive dependencies, includes component identifiers and is linked to a triage and remediation process. SPDX and CycloneDX are common machine-readable formats; the CRA does not prescribe one format.

## E-ITS in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/e-its/
E-ITS is the Estonian information-security framework maintained under RIA. It provides a measure catalogue, a selection method and an audit model. The 2026 version removed preliminary and interim audits and moved to a three-year main audit cycle. E-ITS can support NIS2 evidence but does not by itself prove NIS2 compliance.

## Penetration testing in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/pentesting/
Authorised penetration testing for web applications and APIs; cloud configuration and AI features can be included in an agreed scope. Testing starts only after a written scope and rules of engagement. Deliverables include a findings report with evidence, severity and remediation guidance, plus a retest where agreed. Automated scanners support the work; a person validates every material finding.

## Cybersecurity audit in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/security-audit/
A scoped cybersecurity audit reviews identity and access, configuration, cloud, suppliers, incident readiness and the evidence behind security claims. It is distinct from penetration testing, which attempts controlled exploitation of a specific scope. Deliverables include findings, a management summary and a prioritised remediation plan.

## ISO certification in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/iso-27001/
ISO/IEC 27001 is a voluntary international standard for an information-security management system. Certification is issued by an accredited certification body after a two-stage audit and annual surveillance. It does not by itself prove NIS2, E-ITS or DORA compliance, but it can support the evidence base.

## NIS2 scope assessment (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/nis2/scope-assessment/
Applies when an Annex I or Annex II type of activity meets the size test, or when Article 2(2) names the type regardless of size. Article 2 defines coverage: entities of an Annex I or Annex II type that qualify as medium-sized enterprises or exceed the medium-sized ceilings under the Annex to Recommendation 2003/361/EC and provide services in the Union. Article 3 splits covered entities into essential and important. Recommendation 2003/361/EC supplies the €10m/€50m/€43m ceilings and the 50/250 headcount bands. In Estonia the same test sits in the Cybersecurity Act (KüTS), in force since 1 January 2026. The page carries a browser-only eight-question assessment and a worksheet CSV for recording the decision.

## NIS2 vs ISO 27001 (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/nis2/vs-iso-27001/
An ISO/IEC 27001 certificate cannot prove NIS2 compliance. Certification attests that an information security management system conforms to a voluntary standard; NIS2 is a directive, transposed in Estonia by KüTS and supervised by RIA, and carries duties no management system contains: registration with the competent authority, an early warning within 24 hours and a notification within 72 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident, and board accountability under Article 20. The page maps each Article 21(2) measure to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A controls, shows what an ISMS already supplies, and ships the mapping as a CSV.

## ISO 27001 audit checklist (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/iso-27001/audit-checklist/
An internal audit under clause 9.2 of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 is a planned check of the organisation's own ISMS by people who are not responsible for what they check. It tests conformity with the standard and with the organisation's own rules, and whether the ISMS is effectively implemented and maintained. It is not a certification audit, not a penetration test, and not a policy-library review. The page carries clause 9.2 requirements, a six-step method with sampling defaults, the checklist by Annex A theme, gap scoring, and a 63-row CSV.

## Cybersecurity audit checklist (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/security-audit/checklist/
A cybersecurity audit tests whether the controls an organisation claims to have exist, operate and leave evidence; a penetration test tests whether a specific weakness can be exploited now. The audit reads artefacts — board minutes, access reviews, restore logs, ticket trails, contract schedules — and samples them. The page carries a 74-row checklist across ten domains, sampling guidance, a severity model, and a fill-in report template.

## Penetration test report (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/pentest-report/
A report is useful when a stranger can reproduce each finding and a decision-maker can act on it: scope and rules of engagement, method with a coverage matrix naming what was not tested, one block per finding (identifier, CVSS vector with its scoring version, CWE class, affected asset, evidence, reproduction steps, impact, remediation, retest status), a risk ordering that states its own rule, and an appendix indexing raw tool output. A CVSS base score describes a vulnerability's intrinsic characteristics, not business risk. The page ships a report template and a scope worksheet.

## TLPT and TIBER-EU (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/tlpt/
TLPT is the advanced test DORA Article 26 requires: an intelligence-led, controlled attack on the live production systems behind a financial entity's critical or important functions, at least every three years for entities identified by the competent authority, with independent testers and an attestation route to the supervisor. TIBER-EU is the European framework for running it — developed by the ECB with the national central banks, published in May 2018, updated in 2024 to align with the DORA technical standards on TLPT. TIBER-EE is Estonia's national implementation; Finantsinspektsioon is the TLPT authority for the financial sector. A readiness checklist CSV is published with the page.

## Press and media kit (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/press/

Company facts, boilerplate, founder profile, brand assets, citation formats and media contact for Tehisabiline OÜ. It states that the company offers scoped audits and penetration testing under written authorization, and that the cybersecurity API is in development and not public.
